title: Herzl
hook: Theodor Herzl calls the first Zionist Congress

segments.voice: Yesterday, Dreyfus, and your line: j'accuse. Did you say one true thing out loud? Today, the journalist who was watching in Paris. And a small note: you have come one thousand days up this hill. Day one thousand.

A man in a black beard and a formal coat stands at the front of a hall in Basel, Switzerland. In the seats are Jews from many countries: rabbis and students, doctors and businessmen, people who had never been in one room before. Many came in formal black coats, because he asked them to. He wanted the world to see that this was serious. He wrote plays, and he wrote for a Vienna newspaper. Now he was trying to win his people a state, starting with a meeting. His name is Theodor Herzl, and today's word is his name.
screen: `A HALL IN BASEL.` → `JEWS FROM MANY COUNTRIES.` → `A NATION STARTED WITH A MEETING.`

segments.voice: Herzl had not grown up dreaming of Zion. He was an assimilated Jew in Vienna, writing plays and reporting for a newspaper. What changed him, by his own telling, was what he saw of hatred against Jews, in Vienna and in France. Even Jews who did everything they were asked to do were not safe. So he wrote a short book called The Jewish State. Its argument was blunt: the hatred would not go away on its own, so Jews needed a homeland of their own, recognized by the nations, and they should go about it in the open, with diplomacy, money and organization. Then he did the organizing himself. He called the Zionist Congress in Basel, sought meetings with rulers and their ministers, and wrote letters without end. He also wrote a novel about the future land, and put a motto on its first page. In Hebrew it is known as im tirtzu: if you will it, it is no fairy tale. Here's what makes the motto interesting. It is a dreamer's line, and also a planner's line. The psalm about the return to Zion says, "We were like unto them that dream." Herzl's line agrees that it's a dream, and then insists that wanting it, and working for it, can make it real. Herzl did not live to see a state. And not every Jew agreed with him, not by a long way. Tomorrow you'll meet the many kinds of Zionism, and the Jews who opposed all of them. Today it's enough to see one man turn a longing into an agenda.
screen: `A VIENNA JOURNALIST CHANGES.` · `THE JEWISH STATE.` · `A CONGRESS IN BASEL.` · `A DREAM AND A PLAN.` · then, large: `IF YOU WILL IT, IT IS NO FAIRY TALE.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: dream one practical dream. Sit back and breathe out slowly. Let one hope come up, something you have wanted for a long time and filed under someday. It can be small: a garden, a language, a call you've been meaning to make. Hold it for a moment as a dream. Then turn it over and ask the planner's question: what is the very first step, and when? Find one step small enough to take this week. The bell holds the time.
Herzl. Theodor Herzl, the Vienna journalist who wrote The Jewish State and called the Zionist Congress in Basel. Today's word.
Your line: if you will it. Today, take the first step on your practical dream, and write down the second. Day one thousand.

howItsDone: Herzl is remembered in Israel and in Zionist movements as a founder of political Zionism, and his motto, im tirtzu, if you will it, is often quoted; other Jews, then and now, disagreed with his vision.
